ranking.reasoning: GS revenue growth has been elevated recently (TTM +10.5%, 5Y 17%) driven by trading, IB recovery, and asset management, but base rates suggest reversion toward mid-single-digit growth as capital markets normalize; a downturn scenario (recession, trading slump) could flatten growth near zero. Net margins should stay strong given operating leverage and TTM run-rate near 16-18%, but reverting partially toward the 5Y average with some cyclicality risk from credit losses or market volatility.

BAC's revenue growth will likely normalize toward low-single-digit rates driven by loan growth, NII stabilization, and fee income, after the unusual TTM spike (likely driven by trading/rate effects) fades. Net margins should revert toward the 25-30% historical band as credit costs normalize and rate tailwinds fade, with risks from credit losses, regulatory fines, and a potential recession compressing margins toward the low end.

JPM's revenue growth will normalize from recent NII-driven surges toward low-to-mid single digits as rate tailwinds fade and loan growth tracks GDP, with credit card and trading revenue providing modest diversification; net margins should revert toward the historical 28-31% range as credit costs normalize upward from currently benign levels. Main risks are a credit cycle downturn or recession compressing margins sharply, versus upside from sustained high rates or market share gains in trading/banking fees.

Meta's core ad business continues to benefit from AI-driven engagement and ad targeting improvements plus Reels/WhatsApp monetization, but growth is decelerating from the high-20s toward mid-teens as the base enlarges and digital ad spend matures. Heavy capex for AI infrastructure and Reality Labs losses will pressure margins versus peak 2024 levels, though core efficiency and operating leverage should keep net margins elevated relative to media-industry norms. Main risks include regulatory pressure (EU/Italy fines, privacy rules), intensifying AI capex without proportional revenue return, and

Netflix's growth is decelerating toward mid-to-high single/low-double digits as subscriber saturation in core markets sets in, with ads, price hikes, live sports, and password-sharing crackdowns providing incremental upside; international expansion and gaming remain smaller growth levers. Margins should stay well above historical media norms given content cost leverage and ad-tier scaling, but competitive intensity (Disney, HBO Max, Amazon, YouTube) and content cost inflation cap further margin expansion, so some reversion from TTM peak (29.7%) toward the mid-20s is likely.

UNH retains scale advantages and Optum's diversified growth, but 2024-2025 showed margin compression from medical cost trends, Medicare Advantage repricing pressure, and DOJ/regulatory scrutiny, constraining near-term profitability recovery. Revenue growth should moderate toward mid-single digits as membership growth slows and reimbursement pressures persist, while margins normalize upward from trough levels but stay below the historical ~5-6% net margin peak given structural cost and regulatory headwinds. Key risk: further medical loss ratio deterioration or adverse regulatory/legal action (D

Salesforce's growth has decelerated from historical 20%+ rates to low-double-digits as the CRM market matures, with AI (Agentforce) and M&A (Cresta, Informatica, Slack) providing incremental upside but facing intensifying competition from Microsoft and native AI entrants. Margins should stay near current elevated TTM levels given management's sustained focus on operating leverage and buybacks, though competitive pricing pressure in AI products is a key risk to both growth and margin durability. Main risk: AI disruption could either accelerate seat/consumption growth or commoditize core SaaS va

Oracle's cloud infrastructure (OCI) backlog (RPO) and AI datacenter demand are driving an acceleration from historic high-single-digit growth into the teens, with large contracted capacity providing revenue visibility for several years. The main risk is margin compression from massive capex and debt-financed buildout of GPU capacity, which has lower initial margins than legacy software/licensing, plus execution/financing risk if AI demand growth decelerates or capital costs rise faster than revenue realization.

Pfizer faces a significant patent cliff and post-COVID revenue normalization, with growth likely driven by its oncology pipeline (Seagen) and new launches offsetting losses from Comirnaty/Paxlovid decline and upcoming LOEs (Eliquis, Xtandi). Margins should recover from depressed TTM levels (6-7%) toward historical norms (15-20%) as cost-cutting programs mature and one-time impairments fade, though continued pricing pressure and generic competition remain key risks.

Disney's growth will be driven by parks pricing power, streaming profitability scaling post-restructuring, and ESPN's DTC launch, but linear TV decline remains a persistent drag on the Media networks segment. Margins should recover toward historical norms (~12-14%) as streaming losses turn to profit and cost discipline continues, though content spending cycles and macro-sensitive consumer discretionary spending at parks are key risks.

Alphabet's growth is driven by continued Search/YouTube ad strength, rapid Cloud expansion, and AI-related monetization, but current TTM margins (~50%) are inflated by one-off items like unrealized equity gains and are unlikely to persist given heavy AI capex and depreciation. Base rate reversion plus margin normalization toward the 27-32% historical range is likely as competition, regulatory pressure (antitrust), and capex intensity weigh on returns. Main risk: AI disruption to core Search advertising economics and heavy capex could compress margins faster than growth offsets.

Microsoft's growth is driven by Azure/cloud expansion, AI Copilot monetization, and enterprise software stickiness, with current revenue growth in high teens unlikely to fully persist over five years as base effects and competition weigh in. Heavy capex for AI infrastructure (41% capex CAGR) will pressure margins even as operating leverage from software and cost discipline provide support, so net margin likely moderates slightly from current ~41% TTM toward high-30s. Main risks are AI monetization falling short of massive capex spend, regulatory/antitrust pressure, and macro slowdown denting e

XOM's revenue is heavily tied to oil/gas prices and volumes from Guyana and Permian growth, but is a mature major with low structural growth, so mid-single-digit upside relies on price recovery while downside reflects commodity price collapse or demand destruction. Net margins should revert toward the historical 8-11% range as current elevated refining/upstream margins normalize with oil price and capacity cycles, with the main risk being prolonged low oil prices compressing both revenue and margins simultaneously.

Chevron's revenue is driven by volatile oil & gas prices and production volumes (including Venezuela expansion and LNG demand), so long-term growth should track global energy price cycles and modest production growth rather than any secular trend, with downside risk from a demand/price collapse and upside from sustained high commodity prices. Net margin should revert toward its 5-10yr historical norm (~10%) as current elevated TTM margins reflect cyclical highs rather than a structural improvement, tempered by ongoing capex discipline and cost control.

HD's growth will likely track low-single-digit housing turnover, home improvement spend, and Pro/SRS expansion, with modest recovery as rate cuts potentially boost housing activity, though a severe housing downturn could keep growth near flat. Margins should hold near current ~8.5-9% levels (slightly above TTM's 8.4%) as opex discipline and supply-chain efficiencies offset wage inflation and tariff risks, reverting toward the historical 9-10% norm rather than TTM compression. Main risk: prolonged high mortgage rates suppressing big-ticket remodeling and housing turnover, which is HD's primary

Caterpillar's growth is cyclical and tied to construction, mining, and energy capex, with a record backlog and AI-driven power/data-center demand providing near-term tailwinds, but tariffs, China weakness, and eventual cyclical downturns are key risks over a 5-year horizon. Margins are currently elevated versus history (TTM ~15%) due to pricing and services mix, but should moderate toward the historical 13-14% range as price/cost normalizes and volume cyclicality reasserts itself.

Visa's growth is tied to global payment volume, cross-border travel, and continued displacement of cash, but faces deceleration from a larger base, regulatory/interchange pressure, and competition from real-time payments and fintech disintermediation; a prolonged downturn or adverse regulation could push growth toward the low single digits. Margins are already near structural ceiling given its asset-light network model, so net margin should stay roughly stable with modest reversion from elevated current levels due to increased tech/compliance investment and competitive fee pressure.

Mastercard's growth is driven by continued cross-border travel, e-commerce penetration, and value-added services/data analytics expansion, but double-digit growth of recent years (16% 5Y) is unlikely to fully persist given a larger base, regulatory/interchange pressure, and potential stablecoin/alternative payment rail disintermediation. Margins should stay high given asset-light network economics but may see modest compression from increased investment in new payment rails, AI-driven fraud/compliance costs, and regulatory scrutiny globally. Main risk: faster-than-expected disruption from stab

AWS and advertising growth plus retail operating leverage should sustain high-single to low-double-digit revenue growth, though Amazon's massive revenue base and rising e-commerce/cloud competition make deceleration from current ~15% TTM growth likely. Margins should remain above historical norms due to AWS mix shift and ad revenue, but heavy AI/capex spending and potential retail/cloud price competition create downside risk, so net margin is expected to moderate from the unusually high TTM 16.9% toward a more sustainable ~10-11%.

JNJ's growth is anchored by steady MedTech and pharma demand, with recent launches (oncology, immunology, bipolar drug) and talc litigation resolution providing upside, but patent cliffs (Stelara) and generic competition are key risks to both growth and margin. Net margin should normalize upward from the depressed TTM figure (which reflects one-time litigation/separation charges) toward historical norms as legal overhangs fade, though likely below the unusually high 5Y average due to R&D and pricing pressure.

Apple's growth is driven by Services expansion, installed-base monetization, and AI-enabled product cycles, but is constrained by iPhone maturity and large-base math limiting upside surprises. Margins should stay near current elevated levels given Services mix shift offsetting hardware commoditization, with regulatory/antitrust pressure on Services economics and supply chain/tariff risk as key downside threats to both growth and margin.

Walmart's revenue growth has been steady in the 4-6% range driven by grocery resilience, e-commerce expansion, and advertising/membership income, though scale makes acceleration difficult and base rates favor reversion toward mid-single digits. Net margin should see modest expansion from high-margin ad/membership/fulfillment revenue mix shift, but intense retail competition and grocery's low-margin nature cap upside; main risk is margin pressure from tariffs, wage inflation, or price-based competition with Amazon/Costco/Target.

Costco's growth has been driven by steady membership renewal rates (~90%), new warehouse openings, and e-commerce expansion, though its low-margin model and large revenue base make continued double-digit growth harder to sustain over five years. Net margin should stay structurally thin given the company's cost-plus pricing philosophy, with modest upside from membership fee increases and scale efficiencies offset by competitive pressure from Walmart/Sam's Club and Amazon. Main risk is macro-driven consumer pullback or margin compression from wage/freight inflation.

AMD's data center and AI GPU momentum (MI300/MI350 roadmap, Anthropic deal) plus share gains vs Intel support strong growth, but semiconductor cycles are volatile and competition from Nvidia and custom silicon is intense, so growth could decelerate sharply if AI capex slows. Margins should improve from current TTM levels as data center mix grows and operating leverage kicks in, but reversion toward industry norms and competitive pricing cap upside near high-teens net margin.

Intel's revenue has been roughly flat-to-declining as it loses share in CPUs and struggles to gain traction in foundry/AI accelerators, but easy comps and modest recovery from cyclical lows support low-single-digit growth as the base case, with upside if foundry customers and AI products scale and downside if competitive and execution issues persist. Margins should improve from deeply negative TTM levels as cost cuts, capex discipline, and better utilization kick in, but heavy capital intensity and intense competition from TSMC/AMD/Nvidia likely keep net margins well below Intel's historical m

Tesla's core EV growth has stalled (revenue growth TTM ~8%, quarterly flat) amid rising competition from Chinese automakers and margin compression, but optionality from energy storage, FSD/robotaxi, and new affordable models could reaccelerate growth; base rates suggest reversion toward low-double-digit growth with wide dispersion given execution uncertainty. changeLog.text: Added an automatic accuracy check to every AI breakdown: each percentage, dollar figure and multiple in the text is matched against the computed data and the news the AI was given, and the report shows which figures, if any, couldn't be matched.

The site became a research tool. Stocks, Funds and Crypto each have a lookup that shows performance over 1 day, 10 days, 30 days, year to date, 1 year and 5 years against the market and sector, plus an AI breakdown of why it moved. The paper-trading experiment moved, unedited, to the Track Record tab.

Ended the daily strategy (nightly stock and crypto picks, and the on-demand buttons). Over 159 stock trades it lost $452 while the same dollars in SPY made $13, and its per-trade result versus SPY was below zero with 95% confidence. The September rule change did not fix it, and crypto won 1 of 11. Open trades were closed and the full record stays on this page. The long-horizon track and fund holdings continue.

Crypto now trades seven days a week. A weekend run on Saturday and Sunday means each crypto position is held about one day, instead of Friday's picks sitting until Monday. Same agent, prompt and $500 sizing; stocks are untouched.
When Alpaca refuses to let a stock be shorted (as with ORCL on Oct 8), the bot now records it as skipped instead of as a failed order. The Oct 8 ORCL row stays in the record as it happened.
Fixed a second crypto data bug: the agent was judging each coin on the current, barely started daily bar (about an hour of trading). It now uses the last completed day.

Fixed a data bug: the nightly crypto agent had only been receiving prices for XRP (one of its 10 coins), so it never found a trade. It now sees all 10. Crypto results before this date reflect the bug.

Started a separate long-horizon track: the AI forecasts company fundamentals, code ranks them, and a virtual top-5 portfolio is tracked against SPY. It places no orders and doesn't touch the nightly strategy.
Added a kill switch, a clean-run log, and a dry-run of a $30 live account. Nothing about which trades get made changed.
Shorts now need a specific, stated reason, and the agent is no longer forced to make 3-5 picks a night. Shorts had been the main source of losses.
The direction hit rate is now checked against real prices. The AI's own, more generous grade is shown separately.
Every trade is now compared with simply holding SPY over the same window.
Positions now close by their own share count, with guards so different strategies can't net against each other.
Kept short-side sizing unchanged despite weak results, to avoid acting twice on the same small sample.
Position size is cut in half for low confidence, upcoming events, and shorts, based on the system's own results.
The AI started rating its own confidence on each pick.
Simulated trades can be long or short.

lessons.lessonText: All 11 trades here are "watch whether X extends/continues" framings riding on someone else's cited catalyst (analyst upgrade, sector peer news, macro data point) rather than a primary, firm-specific data event — and all 11 lost, regardless of long/short or confidence. Worth weighing: second-hand narrative catalysts (Ives grouping AAPL with AI names, Cramer citing SpaceX/GPUs, "sector also rallying" framing for JNJ/HD/CAT) may be weaker signals than they appear, since they're sentiment-echo rather than company-specific fundamentals. Also notable: eventRisk=false dominates this batch (9 of 11) yet losses were still frequent and sometimes large (CAT -4.17%, NVDA -2.03%, CRM -2.21%), suggesting the eventRisk flag as currently set isn't capturing the actual risk driving these losses. Sample is small and single-themed (mostly AI/industrial momentum names in one week), so treat this as a narrow pattern, not a general rule.
Shorting stocks that already fell sharply the same day (AMZN -2.2%, GOOGL -3.81%, ORCL -3.1%

Momentum-continuation bets ("watch whether X extends") dominate this batch and lose regardless of direction — both longs chasing a rally and shorts chasing a selloff failed repeatedly (CAT, INTC, ORCL, GS, NVDA, XOM, GOOGL), suggesting the "continuation vs. fade" framing itself isn't adding edge here.

Trades explicitly noting low or below-average volume confirming the move (CAT, INTC x2, ORCL, TSLA) still lost, including some big misses (INTC -6.89%, -5.97%), so "weak volume, likely to fade/reverse" is not a reliable signal in this sample.

Pre-earnings or event-adjacent theses (CRM, ORCL x3, NVDA, AMD) produced some of the largest losses (CRM -15.59%, ORCL -5.99%, -3.90%), hinting that positioning ahead of scheduled catalysts carries outsized tail risk regardless of confidence label.

No clear pattern tied to the confidence field itself — medium and unrated trades both lost similarly, so confidence as recorded doesn't appear predictive here.
